clinical_category: Palliative care in advanced chronic lung disease - concurrent supportive care
blueprint_topic: Interdisciplinary symptom management and goals-of-care support alongside disease-directed treatment
stem: A nurse discusses palliative care consultation with a client who has severe COPD and continues to receive disease-directed treatment. Which explanation is accurate?

options.A: Palliative care can be provided during ongoing treatment to relieve symptoms, support quality of life, and help clarify goals and preferences
options.B: Palliative care should begin only after bronchodilators, oxygen, and other disease-directed treatments have been stopped
options.C: Palliative care is limited to the final days of life and is not appropriate earlier in serious chronic lung disease
options.D: Palliative care replaces the pulmonary and primary-care teams rather than working with them

rationale: A is correct. Current American Thoracic Society patient guidance states that palliative care may be provided at any time during a serious illness, including while the client is receiving medical treatments such as bronchodilators, oxygen therapy, or intensive care. For chronic lung disease such as COPD or IPF, palliative care may address symptoms such as breathlessness and anxiety, and the palliative-care team can help explore the client's values, goals, and preferences. Palliative care specialists work with the client's other health care providers rather than replacing them. B, C, and D therefore conflict with current ATS guidance.
educational_objective: Recognize palliative care as concurrent supportive care that can be integrated throughout serious respiratory illness to manage symptoms, improve quality of life, and support goals-of-care decisions while disease-directed treatment continues.
source_document_title: Palliative Care for People with Respiratory Disease or Critical Illness
source_version_date: ATS Patient Education Series; reviewed February 2024; current resource accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: ATS resource → 'When Should I Receive Palliative Care?': palliative care can be received at any time during illness and while receiving medical treatments including bronchodilators, oxygen therapy, or intensive care. 'Could I Benefit from Palliative Care?': chronic lung disease examples include symptom relief for anxiety and difficulty breathing. 'Who Provides Palliative Care?' and 'What Kind of Care is Right for Me?': palliative specialists work with other providers and help explore values, goals, and preferences.
source_claim_supported: Current ATS guidance directly supports palliative care alongside ongoing disease-directed treatment for serious respiratory illness, including symptom management and goals-of-care support through an interdisciplinary team.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Management of Care client-needs subcategory (15–21% of items), within Safe and Effective Care Environment; this item tests interdisciplinary referral, continuity of care, symptom-support coordination, and goals-of-care communication.
correction_summary: Substantive rebuild. The generic ATS homepage was replaced with the current ATS palliative-care resource and exact sections establishing concurrent use during active treatment, respiratory symptom support, and interdisciplinary goals-of-care work. The final item removes hospice/end-of-life conflation.
audit_findings: The source ATS root URL did not provide an exact palliative-care locator.
The current ATS resource explicitly states that palliative care may be provided throughout illness while disease-directed treatments continue.
The same resource directly supports respiratory symptom relief and exploration of values, goals, and preferences by a team that works with the client's other providers.
The final options clearly distinguish palliative care from hospice-only or treatment-withdrawal-only models without implying that either approach is mandatory.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct answer, no second defensible option, no unsupported prognostic threshold, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
